summary: UML (by Booch, Jacobson and Rumbaugh, 1996; adopted by OMG 1997) is a visual language. Its diagrams are split into **Structure** diagrams (class, object, ...) and **Behaviour** diagrams (use case, activity, sequence, ...).
A class box has 3 compartments: name / attributes / operations. Visibility: `+` public, `-` private, `#` protected, `~` package. **Underlined = static.**

The 5 relationships, from weakest to strongest: dependency (dashed, open arrow) < association (solid line) < aggregation (hollow diamond) < composition (filled diamond). Separate from these: generalisation (solid line, hollow triangle) and realisation (dashed line, hollow triangle).

Mapping to Java: association = a **field**. Dependency = used only as a **parameter, return type or local variable**. Generalisation = `extends`. Realisation = `implements`. Aggregation = parts passed in from outside. Composition = the whole creates its parts with `new`.
Object diagrams show instances as `name : Class`, underlined, and links between them.
Class stereotypes: Entity (stored data), Boundary (UI or interface to the outside), Control (logic that coordinates a use case).
mustMemorise: Visibility: `+` public, `-` private, `#` **protected**, `~` **package** (default, no keyword). `#` is NOT package.
Static attribute or method = **underlined**. Abstract = `{abstract}` (or the name in italics).
Generalisation (`extends`) = **solid** line with a hollow triangle. Realisation (`implements`) = **dashed** line with a hollow triangle. The triangle points at the parent or interface.
An interface extending an interface = **solid** line with a hollow triangle (generalisation), e.g. List to Collection.
Dependency = dashed line with an open arrowhead. Association = solid line (with an open arrowhead if it is navigable one way only).
Dependency: B appears only as a parameter, return type or local variable in A. Association: B is a **field** of A.
The diamond goes at the **whole** end. Hollow = aggregation (parts can exist independently or be shared). Filled = composition (the whole creates and owns its parts, and they die with it).
Multiplicity is written at the far end: `1`, `0..1`, `*` (= `0..*`), `1..*`, `1..5`. Read 'one A has [number at B's end] B's'.
Attribute format: `name : type [multiplicity] = initial-value`. Operation format: `name(direction param : type = default) : returnType`.
Object notation: `objName : Class` underlined. `:Class` = anonymous object. A link is an instance of an association.
Stereotype icons: Entity = circle with a line underneath. Boundary = circle with a T on its left `|-O`. Control = circle with an arrowhead on top.
Naming conventions: Entity = Student/Course. Boundary = xxxUI/xxxForm/xxxInterface. Control = xxxMgr/xxxCtrl/xxxController.

items.title: Why model?
notes: A model is a **simplification of reality**.
Uses: helps visualisation, communication and understanding; used in design creation and investigation; used for documentation.

items.title: Right level of abstraction
notes: Paper airplane = **too abstract to be useful**. Fighter aircraft = the production entity.
A good model sits in between: 'as simple as possible, but not simpler' (Einstein, slide 6).

items.title: UML origins
notes: Created by **Booch, Jacobson and Rumbaugh** (the 'Three Amigos') in **1996**.
**Version 1.1** was adopted by the **OMG** (Object Management Group) in **1997**.
A visual language for **specifying, documenting and communicating** complex software systems. It is not a programming language or a process.

items.title: UML diagram types tree
notes: Hollow-triangle arrows here mean 'is a kind of' (generalisation), so even this chart is drawn in UML.
**Structure** diagrams: Class, Object, Component, Composite Structure, Deployment, Package.
**Behaviour** diagrams: Activity, Use Case, State Machine, and Interaction. Interaction covers Sequence, Communication, Interaction Overview and Timing.
Trap: an **Object diagram is a structure diagram**. **Sequence is an interaction diagram**, which counts as behaviour. Use Case is behaviour.

items.title: Class box: 3 compartments
notes: Top = class name (bold). Middle = attributes, which become Java fields. Bottom = operations, which become Java methods.
Details such as types and visibility may be left out at an early or conceptual stage.

items.title: Attribute and operation syntax
notes: Attribute: `name : type [multiplicity] = initial-value`. For example, `- isPrepaid: Boolean = FALSE` maps to `private boolean isPrepaid = false;`.
`- dateModified: Date [1..*]` means one or more Dates, which maps to an array or collection field.
Operation: `name(parameter-list) : return type`. Parameter: `direction name : type = default`, where direction is `in`, `out` or `inout`.
In UML the type comes **after** the colon (`price: Float`), the reverse of Java's `float price`.

items.title: Association: every label
notes: Shelf `1` to Book `1..*`: one shelf holds 1 or more books, and each book is on exactly 1 shelf. **The multiplicity sits next to the class it counts.**

The open arrowhead at Book means **uni-directional**: Shelf has a field `bookItems` (the **rolename**, which becomes the field name) and Book has no reference back. `{ordered}` is a **constraint** meaning an ordered collection (for example a List).
Person to Person, 'manages': a **reflexive** association, i.e. a class associated with itself. In Java, Person has a Person field. The rolenames manager and subordinate name each end.

Professor `1..2` 'teaches' Course `*`: each course has 1 or 2 professors, and a professor teaches **`*` = `0..*`** courses. The small ▲/◄ beside a name is the **reading direction**, NOT navigability. A plain line with no arrowheads = bi-directional or unspecified.

items.title: Association class (Loan)
notes: Middle diagram: Loan hangs off the Borrower to Equipment line by a **dashed line**. It is an association class: its attribute `date` belongs to the **link**, not to Borrower or Equipment.
Bottom diagram: the same idea promoted to an ordinary class, Borrower `1` to `1..*` Loan `*` to `1` Equipment. Each Loan has exactly 1 borrower and 1 piece of equipment.
Top diagram: Borrower `*` 'loans' Equipment `1..*`, a plain many-to-many with nowhere to store the date.
In standard UML an association class allows only one link per Borrower–Equipment pair. The full Loan class allows repeat loans.

items.title: Aggregation vs composition
notes: The **diamond sits at the WHOLE**: Lecture Group and Family (hollow), Human, Arm and Leg (filled). The plain end is the part.
**Aggregation** (hollow ◇): a whole–part 'has a' relationship with standalone parts that can be shared. A Person is in `*` lecture groups and `1..*` families, and exists without them.
**Composition** (filled ◆): the **whole creates and owns** its parts. Human has `0..2` Arms, and each Arm has `0..1` Hand. The parts' lifetime is tied to the whole.
Both are special kinds of association, so a field in Java (see slide 36).

items.title: Which diamond is which
notes: The red arrows: 'Aggregation' points to the **hollow** diamond (Lecture Group), 'Composition' points to the **filled** diamond (Human).
Think 'containment': stackable boxes = aggregation (a part can be taken out and lives on). Parts sealed inside the whole = composition.
A common mistake is to put the diamond at the part end. It is always at the whole (container) end.

items.title: Generalisation vs realisation
notes: Left: a **solid line with a hollow triangle** pointing at the superclass = generalisation ('is a'), i.e. `class Square extends Rectangle`, `class Rectangle extends Shape`.
Right: a **dashed line with a hollow triangle** pointing at the `<<interface>>` = realisation, i.e. `class BubbleSort implements Sort`.
`<<interface>>` above the name is a stereotype. The interface's methods (sortAscending, sortDescending) must be implemented by each realising class.
Same triangle; only the **line style** differs: solid = extends, dashed = implements.

items.title: Dependency (and the arrow legend)
notes: Legend, top to bottom: filled diamond = composition, hollow diamond = aggregation, solid line with open arrow = association, **dashed line with open arrow = dependency**.
`BenefitsForm --<<call>>--> EmployeeManager`: the tail is the **client** (it depends) and the head is the **supplier** (it is depended on). A change to the supplier may affect the client.
`<<call>>` and `<<use>>` are stereotypes that label what kind of dependency it is. EmployeeManager uses Employee and Benefits.

items.title: Car - - -> ParkingLot = dependency
notes: The car parks in **any** free lot for a while, so there is no lasting link. That is a dependency (dashed line).
Java: ParkingLot appears only as a parameter or local variable, e.g. `void park(ParkingLot lot)`. Car keeps **no field** of type ParkingLot.

items.title: Car ——> ParkingLot = association
notes: The CEO's car has its **own reserved lot**, a lasting structural link, so the line is **solid** (association).
Java: `class Car { ParkingLot myLot; }`, i.e. a **field**. The arrowhead points at ParkingLot because Car knows its lot (navigable from Car).

items.title: Dependency vs association side by side
notes: The two arrows differ **only in the line style**: dashed = dependency, solid = association. Both use the same open arrowhead.
Phone analogy: a payphone you use only for one call is a temporary use (dependency). A phone you always carry is something you hold (association).
Exam rule: if B is held as a field (an instance variable), it is an **association**. If B is used only inside a method (parameter, return type or local variable), it is a **dependency**.

items.title: Abstract class and interface notation
notes: `Shape {abstract}` under the name = abstract class. `areaOf() : float {abstract}` = abstract method. Italic names also mean abstract. Java: `abstract class Shape { abstract float areaOf(); }`. Circle uses a solid line and triangle, so `extends Shape`.
`<<interface>> Observer` with `update(arg : Object)`. TimeObserver uses a **dashed line and triangle**, so `implements Observer`.
`Timer` has a dashed line with an open arrow to Observer = **dependency** (Timer only takes an Observer as a parameter; see slide 37).

items.title: Collections framework: all 3 hollow-triangle uses
notes: The big tabbed box is a **package** (a folder icon) containing the classes.
List to Collection: **solid** line with a hollow triangle = interface **extends** interface (`interface List extends Collection`). It is NOT dashed.

AbstractList to List: **dashed** line with a hollow triangle = realisation (`implements List`). ArrayList to AbstractList: solid line with a triangle (`extends`). `get {abstract}` is abstract in AbstractList, and ArrayList overrides `add` and `get` (shown in the note).

Order to List: dashed line with an open arrow = dependency. Order also lists `lineItems [*]` (a multi-valued attribute), so the slide is a bit loose here; in Java a held `List` field would usually be drawn as an association. Answer by the line style shown.

items.title: Association to Java (fields + multiplicity)
notes: Uni-directional A to B with rolename `myRole` maps to `class ClassA { ClassB myRole; }`. ClassB has no reference to A.
Bi-directional (a plain line, or arrows both ways): **both** classes hold a field.
Multiplicity `1..5` sits at ClassB's end, so each A holds up to 5 Bs: `ClassB[] bObjs = new ClassB[5]` in **ClassA**. `1..10` at A's end gives `ClassA[] aObjs = new ClassA[10]` in **ClassB**.
The link is set up both ways: `new ClassB(this)`, and B's constructor stores `a` in `aObjs`.

items.title: Dependency to Java (3 forms)
notes: A dashed line with an open arrow from A to B means ClassB is used in ClassA **only** as:
1) a method **return type**: `ClassB doSomeThing()`; 2) a method **parameter type**: `doSomeThing(ClassB b)`; 3) a **local variable** inside a method: `ClassB b = new ClassB();`.
None of these is a field. If ClassB were declared as a field, the relationship would be an association.

items.title: Generalisation and realisation to Java
notes: Solid line with a hollow triangle, ClassB to ClassA: `class ClassB extends ClassA`.
Dashed line with a hollow triangle, ClassB to `<<interface>> IInterface`: `class ClassB implements IInterface`.
The arrow always goes from the child or implementer to the parent or interface.

items.title: Aggregation vs composition to Java
notes: Both have a collection **field** `parts` (the rolename). `*` maps to a Vector or ArrayList, or to an array if the size is fixed.
**Aggregation** (hollow ◇): parts come **from outside** by reference, as in `addClassB(ClassB b) { parts.add(b); }`. The parts can outlive A or be shared.
**Composition** (filled ◆): A **creates** its parts itself, as in the constructor `new ClassB()` followed by `parts.add(...)`. The parts live and die with A.
Quick test: where is `new ClassB()` called? Inside the whole = composition. Passed in = aggregation.

items.title: Worked example: diagram to code
notes: Timer has a dashed open arrow to Observer because `notify(Observer o)` uses Observer only as a **parameter**, so the relationship is a dependency, not an association.
`<<interface>> Observer` maps to `public interface Observer { void update(Object arg); }`. Interface methods are implicitly public and abstract.
TimeObserver's dashed line with a hollow triangle maps to `class TimeObserver implements Observer`, which must declare `public void update(Object arg)` (it must be public).
`+` in the diagram maps to `public` in the code.

items.title: Object diagram
notes: An object is written `name : Class` and **underlined** (e.g. `jack : Student`). `[checked out]` is the object's **state**. The lower compartment shows attribute **values** (`title = "Twelfth Night"`).

`:Book` with no name = an **anonymous object**, e.g. `library.checkout(new Book("Twelfth Night"))` with no variable. A plain underlined `b` = an object whose class is not given (the slide pairs it with Java anonymous classes: `new X() { body }`).
The lines labelled takes and teaches are **links**, i.e. instances of associations. There is no multiplicity on links.

items.title: `t.run()` does not start a thread
notes: In the anonymous `Thread` example, `t.run()` just calls `run()` on the **current** thread. Only `t.start()` creates a new thread (checked with JDK 17: it prints `main`).
The point of the code is the anonymous class syntax `new Thread() { ... }`, not threading.

items.title: Visibility symbols and static
notes: `+` public, `#` **protected**, `-` private, `~` **package (default)**. For Java, `~` means no modifier.
**Underlined = static**: `-totalStudents:int` and `+getTotalStudents():int` in Student. `#getID()` is protected and `~getEmailAddress()` is package-private.
Constructors are shown with no return type: `+Employee(String)`. Parameters may be shown as types only, `changeName(String):void`.
`<<enumeration>> DayOfWeek` with literals Sunday, Monday, Tuesday maps to a Java `enum`. `:DayOfWeek [Sunday]` is an instance of it, shown in object notation.

items.title: Employee: static getter, non-static field
notes: `+getNextID():int` is underlined (static), but `-nextID:int` is **not** underlined (an instance field). `+STARTING_PAY_RATE` (a constant name) is not underlined either.
In Java a static method cannot read an instance field. JDK 17 gives 'non-static variable nextID cannot be referenced from a static context'. `nextID` should be underlined too.
Exam: go strictly by the notation. Only underlined members are static, so in this diagram only `getNextID()` is static.

items.title: Class stereotypes: Entity, Boundary, Control
notes: **Entity** (circle sitting on a line): **persistent information** tracked by the system (think database).
**Boundary** (circle with a T on its left, `|-O`): interaction between the system and the outside world, i.e. **interfaces** (UI, devices).
**Control** (circle with an arrowhead on top): **logic** that coordinates and realises a use case.

items.title: Stereotype naming conventions
notes: Entity: Student, Course, Group (nouns from the problem domain).
Boundary: xxxUI, xxxForm, xxxInterface, e.g. **InvoiceForm**.
Control: xxxMgr, xxxCtrl, xxxController, e.g. **CourseMgr**.

items.title: Stereotypes applied to the dependency example
notes: BenefitsForm = **Boundary** (UI). EmployeeManager = **Control**. Employee and Benefits = **Entity** (stored data).
Typical flow: Boundary `<<call>>`s Control, and Control `<<use>>`s the Entities. Every arrow is a dashed dependency with the client at the tail and the supplier at the head.

items.title: Summary: the relationship notation table
notes: Dependency: dashed line, open arrow. Association: solid line, open arrow. Aggregation: solid line, hollow diamond. Composition: solid line, filled diamond. Generalisation: solid line, hollow triangle. Realisation: dashed line, hollow triangle.
Nesting: dependency is the most general. Association is a kind of dependency, aggregation a kind of association, composition a stronger aggregation. 'w/p' = whole/part.
Stereotype icons, left to right: Boundary, Control, Entity.

items.title: Interface lollipop; instance specification
notes: An interface can be drawn as a box marked `<<interface>>` OR as a **lollipop** (a small circle on a stick).
An instance is written `myAddress : Address`, with the **whole name underlined**. A line between two instances (Don : Person, father to son, Josh : Person) is a **link**.

items.title: Navigability and end properties
notes: An open arrowhead at an association end = that end is **navigable**. A small **x** = **not navigable**.

Things written near the end of a line: the end name (rolename), the multiplicity, and properties in `{}`: `{ordered}` (ordered set), `{bag}` (duplicates allowed), `{sequence}`/`{seq}` (ordered with duplicates).
A **link** = an instance of an association.

items.title: Composition, dependency, generalisation (official definitions)
notes: Composition: a part belongs to **at most one composite at a time**. If the composite is deleted, its parts are normally deleted too.
Dependency: the client needs the supplier. **Changing the supplier may affect the client.** CarFactory dashed-arrow to Car = an 'instantiate' dependency (the factory creates Cars).
Generalisation hierarchies must be **directed and acyclic** (no class may inherit from itself, even indirectly).

items.title: Realisation vs usage look-alikes
notes: Interface realisation and realisation are both a **dashed line with a hollow triangle**. A classifier may implement many interfaces; these are its 'provided interfaces'.
Usage `<<use>>` is a **dashed line with an open (stick) arrowhead**, which is a dependency (Order needs LineItem).
Look at the arrowhead: hollow triangle = realisation, open stick = dependency.

items.title: Association class and comment
notes: Association class (Job with a salary, between Person and Company): its features belong to the **relationship**. It is attached to the association line by a dashed line.
Comment = a dog-eared note box joined by a dashed line. It **carries no semantic force**.

items.title: Constraints
notes: A constraint is written in `{ }`, e.g. `size: Integer {size >= 0}`, or placed in a note. `{xor}` across two associations means only one of them can hold (an Account belongs to a Person XOR a Corporation).
The predefined language for writing constraints is **OCL** (Object Constraint Language).
